parole.testo: Unknown. Several theories exist: * Of Baltic origin (compare Latvian sakas and Lithuanian šaka). * From Proto-Germanic *hakkōną. * From the same source as Lithuanian šokti. * From the same source as Finnish häkä.

Cognate to Finnish allikko. Possibly from a Baltic language, compare Lithuanian šaltenis (“spring”) and šaltinis (“spring, source, that which is cold”). While the expected initial h- is seen in older Estonian texts, its loss in Finnish is unexplained, possibly due to similar words starting with ala-
Borrowed from a Baltic language, compare Lithuanian kaimas. and Latvian ciems. Cognate to Finnish kaima.
From a Baltic language. Compare Lithuanian bristi (“to wade”) (1st person singular present brendu). Cognate to archaic Finnish rentiä.

parole.significato: aftergrass, aftermath (regrown grass after mowing or grazing)
parole.testo: Derived from a Baltic language, compare Latvian atāls, Lithuanian atólas and Old Prussian attolis. Cognate with Livonian addõl (“aftermath”).
